rationale: Set A wins because it finds the real nerve in this launch: "Deel's compliance tool is a bet that AI can read 150 countries' labor law — with no accuracy numbers." That is a reporter's question, not a brochure in a trench coat. Set B has useful bones, but "Deel bets AI can flag contractor-misclassification risk across 150 countries" drifts into category-creation optimism and claims Deel is "turning" payroll data into a risk engine, which the facts do not say.
gaps_in_A: "Deel is giving away the compliance layer it used to sell" overstates the facts. The update says the tool is included for existing customers; it does not say Deel previously sold this layer separately or that pricing will not change at renewal.
"compresses the ground under standalone compliance vendors" is a plausible market hypothesis, not a grounded claim. It needs competitor pricing or buyer evidence before it becomes pitchable.
The next step, "newsjack-detector," is not the cleanest immediate move. The sharper first move is to get accuracy/audit data and one customer use case; without those, even the best angle limps.
gaps_in_B: "turning that into a real-time classification risk engine" invents the data path. Deel handles payroll and compliance for thousands of companies, but the update does not say the tool uses that customer data.

"Deel ships a free compliance AI while fighting a corporate-espionage lawsuit" is a real conflict angle, but it is litigation-adjacent gasoline. It needs court-record fact-checking before anyone pitches a syllable of it.
"Remote, Rippling" are unsupplied named competitors. Fine as private beat context if verified, sloppy as an asserted outlet map inside a grounded angle set.

"raises switching costs and pressures rivals who'd charge for the same capability" stacks inference on inference. The set admits it needs competitor or analyst proof, but the angle headline still walks in like the proof already exists.
